rendered: The NFA hydroxide precursors must be coprecipitated within a narrow pH window of[1] 10 and 12[2]. The reason is that aluminum hydroxide starts precipitating at a lower pH than nickel and iron hydroxides, which precipitate only beyond pH[3] 6[4]. Because the solubility product (Ksp) of the resulting hydroxide precipitates differs among these metals, simultaneous coprecipitation of Ni, Fe and Al is challenging, which narrows the usable window.[5] In practice, a continuous stirred tank reactor is fed with metal sulfates, carbonates or chlorides plus a chelating agent, and NaOH is pumped in to keep the pH above[6] 10[7], especially for nickel-rich materials. To turn the precursors into cathode powder, the reactor outflow is filtered, washed and dried to obtain the hydroxide precursors, which are mixed with a lithium source (Li2CO3, LiOH, LiNO3, etc.) and calcined in an O2-rich environment at temperatures above[8][9] 600[10] °C. The resulting NFA cathode powders are then cast into electrodes by roll-to-roll slot-die coating and assembled into pouch cells.[11]
